transcript:
Header:
Date: 2025-09-04
Start: 16:00 PT
Duration: 41 mins
Record: Yes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam Patel (Redwood SE), Ava Gomez (Redwood DevAdv), Evan Torres (Quicksilver CTO), Priya Naidu (Lead ML Eng), Samir Khan (Platform Eng), Rita Flores (PM)
---
Auto-summary: Quick SDK orientation for Quicksilver's dual-language monorepo. Focus on auth patterns, sandbox provisioning, CI secrets, and using Redwood Optimize to reduce token cost. Discussed dedicated vs hosted and private VPC options for PII-sensitive workloads.
---
00:00 Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Maya, I run the account here. we'll do a quick... um orientation on the SDKs, a short Console walkthrough and then Liam will demo Optimize suggestions. If at any point shout out questions.
00:12 Evan: Thanks Maya, appreciate it. We're trying to move from a prototype on OpenAI to something more predictable cost/latency wise, and want to see how Redwood fits.
00:20 Maya: Great, can you remind us of your immediate success criteria? Latency? cost per 1k tokens? data residency?
00:28 Priya: Yeah, primary is latency for our real-time code-assist feature, target P95 around 250ms for 64-token responses. Second is cost — we want to lower per-token cost without losing quality — and third is data controls, some of our customers require EU residency.
00:45 Liam: Cool, thanks. Quick clarifying q: are you running models in-house now or on hosted endpoints?
00:52 Samir: Right now everything's on OpenAI with a small VM-based cache layer. We're trying to centralize inference in a service and may do a Dedicated pool if the numbers work.
01:05 Maya: Good, that'll shape the pilot. We'll show both hosted flow and how Dedicated and Private VPC would look. Ava will start with the SDK quickstart.
01:15 Ava: Ok, I'll share my screen? (screen share starts) So in the repo we usually drop the SDK in a top-level package. For Python use pip install redwood-inference and for TS npm i @redwood/inference, examples in the quickstart folder. The quickstart uses REDWOOD_API_KEY env var or you can use service account JSON for CI.
01:36 Priya: Service account — how does that map to SSO? We have SAML SSO and want team-level roles.
01:44 Liam: Right, we support SSO for the Console and can mint short-lived creds via our private control plane for Private customers; for hosted, service accounts are long-lived keys you'd store in your secret manager. The Console also supports SAML provisioning and RBAC.
01:58 Speaker 1: (muted) um sometimes the token rotation is automatic if you use the service account flow, otherwise you rotate keys via the console.
02:07 Samir: For CI we need a pattern that doesn't leak keys in PRs — do you have a recommended approach?
02:12 Ava: Yes, we recommend using ephemeral sandbox tokens for dev branches — you can provision sandboxes in the Console and bind them to a minimal role. For CI, use your secrets manager (HashiVault, AWS Secrets Manager, GitHub Actions secrets) and inject at runtime. We have a small GH Actions example in the quickstart: action sets REDWOOD_API_KEY from secrets and the runner uses the TS client.
02:34 Priya: Can you show the GH Action snippet?
02:38 Ava: Sure (scrolls). Example line:
  - name: Set Redwood key
    env:
      REDWOOD_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.REDWOOD_API_KEY }}
  - run: npx ts-node ./scripts/run_inference.ts
02:52 Priya: Cool. For the service account JSON, do you store it raw in secrets manager? because we have strict audit around what can be stored.
03:01 Liam: For Private deployments, customers can integrate with KMS/HSM and rotate keys via their KMS; in hosted we integrate with KMS on our side but give you audit logs and optional HSM for keys. We can send SOC 2 and encryption docs — Maya will share.
03:17 Maya: Yep, security pack going out after the call.
03:22 Evan: Walk us through Optimize — you mentioned automatic batching and quantization recs.
03:27 Liam: Right, quick demo. (switches to console) The Optimize tab analyzes traffic patterns and recommends batch sizes, KV cache TTL, and quantization profiles per model. For example, for a high short-seq workload like yours, Optimize suggested small batch sizes but aggressive KV caching, because you reuse prefixes heavily. It also shows estimated cost delta — e.g., 18% token cost reduction with adaptive batching + int8 quantization.
03:55 Priya: When you say int8 quantization, do you do that online or is it a model artifact we have to pin?
04:02 Liam: It's a serving-time config — we use quantized kernels; some models have multiple quantized variants pinned in the model catalog. If you pin a variant we will route to that variant; otherwise Optimize can recommend model family + quant profile to test in canary.
04:19 Rita: Any recs for quality regressions with quant? We've seen hallucination changes when moving low-precision.
04:26 Liam: Yep, that's why we tie Optimize suggestions to eval sets. You upload a small prompt set, Optimize runs a scoring pass and flags quality regressions. We run A/B canary with automatic rollback on quality drop.
04:40 Maya: Sounds like a fit. Let's circle back to integration specifics for a monorepo. Ava?
04:46 Ava: In a mono-repo we suggest a single auth layer that maps to team roles. For the TS frontend, use a minimal proxy that exchanges short-lived tokens for the browser (never embed the server key). For server-side functions use the SDK directly with the service account. We included a reference architecture in the deck: link: https://redwood.ai/decks/quicksilver-onboard (note: sample link).
05:10 Evan: About latency — you'd mentioned dedicated GPU pools; what are the expected P95 numbers for 64 tokens?
05:16 Liam: On a Dedicated A100 pool we typically see P95 sub-100ms for optimized models at 64 tokens with batching tuned; hosted multi-tenant can be higher depending on load, usually 120-220ms P95. There's some variance with sequence length and KV cache.
05:33 Priya: That sounds promising. We need a real-world bench — can you share a runner we can run against our dataset?
05:38 Liam: Yes, I'll attach a small benchmark script in Python that iterates 1k sample prompts, records latency and token usage. We recommend running it in your staging environment pointing to a sandbox key so we can reproduce.
05:49 Samir: About VPC: for EU residency, can you pin region? And what's the deployment model for Private?
05:56 Maya: For hosted you can choose region endpoints; for Private we deploy into your VPC or on-prem package. Data residency in EU is supported via dedicated region and private control plane. We'll include the Private deployment checklist in the security pack.
06:12 Evan: Ok, let's talk errors and observability — what do the logs look like?
06:17 Liam: In Console we have token-level breakdowns per request, per-route cost, latency histograms, trace hooks and error traces. You can forward logs to Datadog or Sumo for unified observability. We also emit structured events for each call: model, tokens_in/out, latency_ms, error_code. (audio overlap)
06:40 Priya: Do you keep raw prompts in the logs? We have PII concerns.
06:43 Liam: By default we redact prompt text in logs for hosted mode; customers can opt into fuller logs in Private deployments with customer-managed storage. We also support retention policies.
06:56 Rita: What's the SLA for Dedicated?
06:59 Maya: Typical SLA is 99.9% with latency SLOs per contract; Dedicated customers get priority capacity and can configure autoscale policies.
07:09 Evan: Any migration support? We have some internal infra engineers, but would prefer a co-pilot to help during pilot.
07:15 Maya: Definitely, our Solutions team does the pilot onboarding. We'll do a 4-week pilot with an AE, SE, and an on-call support window.
07:25 Ava: I'll demo the SDK flows now — quick code. (shares terminal) Python:
  from redwood import Client
  client = Client(api_key=os.environ.get('REDWOOD_API_KEY'))
  resp = client.generate(model='rw-2.0-opt', prompt='Summarize...')
In TS:
  import { Redwood } from '@redwood/inference'
  const client = new Redwood({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY })
  const res = await client.generate({ model: 'rw-2.0-opt', input: '...' })
07:52 Priya: You referenced model names — sometimes our prompts require a different family; can Optimize recommend a lighter family for lower cost?
07:58 Liam: Yes, Optimize will suggest compatible families and estimate quality delta. It also proposes LLM quantization profiles. Note that not all open families have int8 support; it depends on model architecture.
08:13 Evan: Regarding rollout — can we do canary and automatic fallback?
08:16 Liam: Yes, rollouts support traffic splits, canaries, and fallback policies to a cheaper model if error or latency spikes. You can pin versions too.
08:25 Samir: About caching — KV cache for code-assist is important. How persistent is it across sessions?
08:30 Liam: KV caching is per-session with configurable TTL. For prefix-heavy workloads we keep long TTLs and share caches across instances when appropriate. There was a small transcription glitch: sometimes the console shows "K V cash" but it is KV cache.
08:45 Priya: Any quota or rate limit concerns? Our burst patterns are spiky during business hours.
08:50 Maya: You can configure rate limits and burst capacity; Dedicated can be configured with reserved throughput and burst credits. Also we support traffic shaping rules.
09:00 Ava: Quick note on cost visibility — Console breaks down cost per token, model, and route. The Optimize tab simulates cost after applying batching and quantization recommendations.
09:12 Evan: Great. Can we see a live example of the Optimize suggestion pipeline on a small dataset?
09:18 Liam: I'll trigger a small run — I have a sample eval set we run. (loads sample) The UI shows suggestions: increase batch to 8 for background jobs, batch to 2 for real-time; enable KV cache TTL 30s; quantize to int8 for model-rw-2.0-opt-v2, estimated cost -17% and latency +12% for some requests. It also scores quality delta: BLEU-like metric down 0.8% on eval set.
09:50 Priya: 0.8% drop might be acceptable if quality metrics indicate. Can we run A/B on a percentage of traffic?
09:55 Liam: Yes, set canary at 10% and Evaluate over the next 24 hours; automatic rollback if quality drops beyond threshold.
10:05 Rita: Ok, process question — procurement will ask for security docs and SOC2. We'll need that before legal signs off.
10:10 Maya: We'll send SOC 2 + ISO docs and an architecture whitepaper. Also share the legal contact for standard data processing addendum.
10:20 Evan: Any hidden egress costs if we use Private?
10:24 Maya: For Private, egress within your VPC is your cloud egress; Redwood charges platform fee and support, but compute is in your environment so egress follows your cloud billing. We'll detail it in the pricing workbook.
10:36 Samir: How do we handle model updates? We want reproducible inference for A/B tests and audits.
10:41 Liam: You can pin model version hashes; the Console keeps model provenance and rollout history. We also provide a snapshot export for audit.
10:52 Priya: Are there sample manifests to define model pinning per route?
10:55 Ava: Yes, repo has a redwood.json manifest sample. Example: {"routes": [{"name":"code-assist","model":"rw-2.0-opt@v23-07"}]} (note: transcription may show braces flattened).
11:14 Evan: Ok, this is good. Let's recap real quick and confirm owners.
11:19 Maya: Recap: Redwood to send security pack + pricing workbook. Liam to share benchmark runner gist. Quicksilver to supply 1k prompt samples and SLOs. Schedule pilot kickoff week of 9/15.
11:32 Priya: I'll pull a sample set and share by 9/8.
11:37 Maya: Perfect. Any final Qs?
11:40 Evan: One small one — how do you support multi-tenant routing for customers who serve multiple clients?
11:45 Liam: We recommend per-tenant routing at the application layer with token scoping; Redwood Console supports per-route billing and per-token cost attribution. Support for per-tenant isolation via Dedicated pools is common.
11:57 Rita: Thanks everyone, good session.
12:00 Maya: Thanks, we'll follow up with links. Meeting adjourned.
